opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the RNN analogy is actually a really nice way into it. In a classic RNN, you have one block of weights that you apply over and over again, and each time you apply it you carry forward a hidden state. The recurrence there is along the sequence: you read token one, update your state, read token two, update your state, and so on. The same parameters get reused at every step.

What we do with recurrent depth is take that same idea of reusing a block, but turn it ninety degrees. Instead of recurring over the sequence dimension, we recur over the depth dimension. So you still have a normal transformer that processes all the tokens in parallel with attention, but in the middle of the model there's a core block of layers that we loop. You embed your input into a latent state, then you feed that state through the same core block again and again, maybe four times, maybe thirty-two times, and only at the end do you decode it back out into a prediction for the next token.

So the hidden state in an RNN corresponds to this latent state that's being refined at every iteration, and the time steps of the RNN correspond to iterations of thinking for a single token. The nice property that falls out of this is that compute is decoupled from parameter count. You have a fixed number of weights, but at test time you can decide to run more iterations, and if the model was trained the right way, it gets better at harder problems by simply thinking longer in that latent space, without having to write out a long chain of thought in tokens.

There are some details that make it work in practice. For example, we re-inject the input embedding at every step, a bit like how an RNN gets fresh input at each time step, so the model doesn't forget what it was supposed to be working on. And during training we randomly sample the number of iterations, so the model learns to produce something useful whether it gets a few steps or many. But the core intuition really is: it's an RNN, except the thing it's recurring over is its own reasoning about the current position, rather than the next word in the sentence.

r001.rationale: The response says recurrent depth repeats a core block over latent state and compares iterations to thinking for a single token, but it also says the transformer processes all tokens in parallel. It does not clearly convey repeated computation at the current sequence position before advancing to the next token.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I like to think about it is: a standard RNN is recurrent in time. You have some hidden state, you feed in one token, you update the state, you feed in the next token, you update the state again, and so on. The same set of weights gets applied over and over, once per position in the sequence. The recurrence runs along the sequence axis.

What we're doing with recurrent depth is basically taking that same idea and rotating it ninety degrees. Instead of recurring along the sequence, we recur along the depth of the network. So you have a block of transformer layers, and rather than stacking, say, forty distinct blocks with forty distinct sets of weights, you take one block and you apply it repeatedly. The output of the block gets fed back in as the input, together with the original embedding of the token, and you iterate. Every iteration is like one time step of an RNN, except the "time" here is the number of times you've refined the representation, not the position in the text.

And just like an RNN carries a hidden state that gets updated step by step, here the latent state for each token gets updated step by step. The state at iteration zero is pretty rough; the state at iteration eight or sixteen or thirty-two has had more compute poured into it and, ideally, has converged to something more useful. So you can think of it as the model "thinking" in latent space for a variable number of steps before it commits to an output.

The nice property that falls out of this analogy is the same one that makes RNNs appealing in the first place: the number of steps isn't fixed at training time. An RNN doesn't care how long your sequence is; you just keep unrolling. Our model doesn't care how deep you unroll it; you just keep iterating. So at test time, you can decide, for this token, I'll do four iterations, and for this harder token, I'll do sixty-four. You get adaptive compute per token without any change to the parameter count.

The other thing the analogy helps with is training. People know that training RNNs over very long sequences is hard, you get vanishing gradients, you have to truncate backprop through time. We hit exactly the same issue along depth. So we borrowed the same trick: we sample a random number of iterations during training, and we only backpropagate through the last few of them, truncated backprop through depth, essentially. The earlier iterations run forward without gradient. That keeps the memory cost bounded, and it also forces the model to learn a state update that's stable and keeps improving no matter where it gets dropped in, because it never knows at which iteration the gradient is going to start.

So if you want the one-sentence version: it's an RNN where the recurrence happens over computation steps instead of over tokens, and that gives you a transformer that can scale its depth at inference time the way an RNN scales its length.

r001.rationale: The response says recurrence happens over computation steps rather than tokens and that each token’s latent state is updated iteratively, but it does not clearly say that computation repeats at the current sequence position before advancing to the next token.

astra-6.text:
Think of an RNN as repeatedly applying the same computation to a hidden state. Usually, that recurrence runs over a sequence: you read a token, update the state, read the next token, and so on. In recurrent depth, we take that same idea and run the recurrence along the depth of the model instead.

So you embed the input, then pass its hidden representation through a shared transformer block repeatedly. Each pass updates that representation, giving the model another opportunity to work on the same input before producing an answer. If you unroll those iterations, it looks like a deep transformer, except the layers share weights.

The interesting consequence is that you can separate the number of parameters from the amount of computation. You can run more iterations without adding more parameters. Conceptually, that gives the model a way to spend more time thinking in its hidden state, rather than having to express every additional step as another output token. Whether those extra iterations actually help is something the model has to learn.

r001.rationale: The response says recurrent depth repeatedly updates the same input along model depth, but it does not clearly state that this computation repeats at the current sequence position before advancing to the next token.

sol-6.1.text:
Think of an RNN as applying the same computation repeatedly, carrying a hidden state from one step to the next. Usually, those steps correspond to different tokens in a sequence. With recurrent depth, we take that idea and apply it along the depth of the model instead. We reuse the same block of layers, and each time through, it updates the hidden representation of the same input.

So instead of moving to the next word, you’re taking another computational step on the words you already have. That gives you a way to spend more computation on an input without adding more parameters: you can run that shared block more times. The interesting question then is whether the model learns to use those additional steps to refine its answer.

r001.rationale: The response says recurrent depth repeats a shared block on the same input and contrasts this with moving to the next word, but it does not clearly describe repeatedly computing at the current sequence position before advancing to the next token.
